doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Early listening: Motown, Latin, Caribbean music and church hymns
summary: Daley grew up on the Lower East Side with Motown, Latin and calypso; his Montserrat parents sang Anglican anthems.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Can you remember when you were in let’s say your early teens. What was the music that you would have bought LPs for?
Junior high school or high school?

Well junior high school, you know, Motown records were very very popular then so it would be some selection of Motown. And then I grew up in the lower east side of Manhattan and Latin music was very popular so you know the music of Tito Puente, you know, those type of, Eddie Palmieri and everything. I would definitely participate. And then my family is from the Caribbean. My parents came from Montserrat British West Indies, so we always had a lot of calypsos and those types of music from the Caribbean too. So it was a combination of Caribbean music, you know, Latin music that surrounded me in the neighborhood that I grew up in, and then popular music and everything. Unfortunately at that age I was not listening to jazz. I didn’t get into jazz until high school. You know so, and my parents were not into jazz either. So they listen. My mother’s music and my father’s music was mainly the music of the church. And we are © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Episcopalian so it wasn’t the Gospel music, but the anthem, the Anglican anthems. We mainly sang those type of things, is the kind of music that my parents listened to.

When you were in church singing those hymns, do you remember what might have been going through your head as far as, I’m not sure how to phrase this question, were you wanting to move away from the written note?

No. No. In an Episcopalian upbringing, no. My mind was you better not move away from that, no. My mother was not a big fan of Gospel music. She thought it was, you know, because you’ve got to realize that you know, Montserrat was colonized by the British. And they, you know the British are very very strict and stern and most western music came out of islands that were colonized from the British were very very conservative and in church you sang the hymn like it was written. You did not venture forth or move away from any, or bend a note or any type of thing. And the structure harmonically was four part harmony similar to the chorales of Bach, you know, four part harmony, Bach. Bach chorales and other things that were used to harmonize the different melodies that we sang.
